coverage.hazard.heat_wave.label: ERA5 climate reanalysis, crop heat scale

detail.what: How hot a place runs for crops: where its temperature sits in the crop's heat-stress band, and how unusually hot the year is against the 1991–2020 normal. Read from the ERA5 climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against observed cocoa production in West Africa (FAO and ICCO), a record independent of the climate data: over 34 years, rank agreement 0.60.
detail.next: Validated for cocoa only. Bordeaux wine grapes showed no heat signal (0.01). A crop heat-stress scale, not a measure of heat damage to buildings.

detail.what: The number of days a year above 30 °C, counted from 30 years of daily maximum temperatures (NASA POWER).
detail.why: Checked against hot days counted at 248 weather stations in Europe and the United States (NOAA GHCN-Daily, 1991–2020), which the data source does not use: rank agreement 0.92.
detail.next: Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports. It counts hot days; it is not a damage estimate.

detail.what: Two scores. Cold wave: how far the 1-in-10-year coldest night falls below the point where pipes freeze and below the cold a building was designed for, from 30 years of daily minimum temperatures (NASA POWER). Frost: the coldest night of the coldest month, on a crop scale.
detail.why: The cold-wave score was checked against the coldest nights at 248 weather stations in Europe and the United States (NOAA GHCN-Daily, 1991–2020): rank agreement 0.89.
detail.next: The frost score is a crop scale and is not used as a building hazard. Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports.

coverage.hazard.wildfire.label: Copernicus fire weather and satellite burn history

detail.what: How often fire weather reaches extreme danger (Copernicus Fire Weather Index, 2006–2020), weighted by the share of land that can burn, plus the burn history seen by satellite (ESA Climate Change Initiative, 2001–2019). A fixed, published formula.
detail.why: Checked on the official European burn record (EFFIS, 41,000 burn scars) for 2022–2024, later than every input: it finds burned places with a hit rate of 0.76 and ranks burned area with rank agreement 0.37, just above the {bar} bar. Gridded burned-area records also pass in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Oceania.
detail.next: Most of the skill comes from past burn history, which overlaps the test record; fire weather and fuel alone reach 0.68 and 0.22. In North America gridded burned area passes but fire-perimeter records fall just short. A same-day fire-weather version did not pass (0.44) and is not used.

detail.what: How much a place warms under a climate scenario, against today's climate, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year; it has no value for today. Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How far apart the warmest and coldest months lie, and how much the year-to-year values spread, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: It describes the climate rather than a damage, so testing it against weather stations would prove nothing.
detail.next: Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: The probability that the ground at a place is permafrost, from the published 1 km northern-hemisphere permafrost map (Obu et al., 2019).
detail.why: Checked against ground temperatures measured in 229 boreholes of the Global Terrestrial Network for Permafrost, never used to build the map: rank agreement 0.82, well above the {bar} bar.
detail.next: Northern hemisphere only, from 25° north; Central Asia and Tibet have 12 boreholes, too few to judge. It shows where permafrost is, not the damage from its thaw.

detail.what: The 1-in-10-year wind speed at a place from tropical cyclones, modelled from every storm track recorded since 1981 in IBTrACS, the international best-track archive.
detail.why: Rebuilt from the storm seasons before a test window and checked on the storms that came after: rank agreement 0.78 to 0.88 across five windows of at least 10 seasons.
detail.next: A test of wind strength, not of damage: observed wind damage and insured losses are not tested yet. The score and the test come from the same track archive, split in time. Europe's sample is thin (30 places).

detail.what: How strong the yearly peak wind gusts are at a place, from the ERA5 climate reanalysis: the European winter windstorms, blizzards and dust storms that tropical-cyclone models miss.
detail.why: Checked against peak gusts measured at 92 weather stations (NOAA): rank agreement 0.57 overall, 0.79 in Europe (34 stations) and 0.38 in North America (58 stations, a narrow pass).
detail.next: It ranks places by gust hazard; it is not a loss model. Against NOAA's reported gusts it reaches 0.26, and against US damaging-event counts 0.05, so no euro figure is published for it.

detail.what: How much near-surface wind speed changes at a place under a climate scenario, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models. A rise and a fall both count.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year. Context only: it never leads a headline.

coverage.hazard.tornado.label: ERA5 storm instability and wind shear

detail.what: How often the air above a place has the instability and wind shear that breed tornadoes, large hail and damaging winds, from a published severe-storm index (Taszarek, 2021) on the ERA5 climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against 70,000 tornadoes recorded by NOAA's Storm Prediction Center: it finds them with a hit rate of 0.73 (0.74 for the stronger ones). Rebuilt from earlier years, it reaches 0.82 on later ones.
detail.next: It describes the storm environment, not damage: it does not rank US counties by reported damage (0.09).

detail.what: How much drier than normal a place is, from the SPEI drought index: rainfall set against the water that evaporation takes.
detail.why: Checked against observed crop-production shocks (FAO) over 34 years in 21 crop regions. It holds for rain-fed winter cereals and tree crops in dry climates: Australian wheat (0.64), North African wheat (0.47 to 0.67), West and Central Asian wheat (0.40 to 0.57) and central Spain (0.56).
detail.next: Not a general drought score: it does not hold for humid, irrigated or summer crops, such as the US Corn Belt, Brazil, Argentina, Indian rice and cane, Nigeria and South Africa.

detail.what: The share of a place inside the 1-in-100-year river floodplain, and the damage expected at its average flood depth, from the JRC river-flood maps (Copernicus Emergency Management Service, 90 m): the European maps in the countries they cover, the global maps outside them.
detail.why: Checked on the flood extents Copernicus mapped in six floods from 2019 to 2024, none of which the maps were built from: rank agreement 0.74 across 144 mapped places, hit rate 0.84. Floods are found well (hit rate 0.81 to 0.87); the Ahr flash flood less so (0.62).
detail.next: River flooding only: surface-water, flash and groundwater floods are not covered, and coastal flooding is its own hazard. The maps assume no flood defences. It does not rank US places by flood-insurance claims (0.08): a hazard score, not a loss model.

detail.what: How dry the soil around plant roots normally is at a place, compared with other land, from the ERA5-Land climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against the loss of water stored on land seen by NASA's GRACE satellites from 2002 to 2026, at 3,124 places: rank agreement 0.08, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Observed water loss is driven by groundwater pumping, reservoirs and snow, which a soil-dryness score does not model.

coverage.hazard.sea_level_rise.label: Tide gauges and IPCC sea-level rise

detail.what: How high a site stands above the 1-in-10-year extreme sea level observed at the nearest tide gauge (GESLA-3, 1,864 gauges, 1979–2020), with the sea-level rise the IPCC Sixth Assessment projects and its likely range.
detail.why: The extreme level rebuilt from gauge years up to 2010 ranks the peaks the same gauges recorded from 2011 to 2020 with rank agreement 0.92 (810 gauges). At US gauges, the score ranks the peaks observed from 2014 to 2023 at 0.41 (218 gauges).
detail.next: A test of extreme still-water levels, not of flood depth or damage. Sites with no gauge within 250 km are not scored. The gauge network is densest in Europe and North America.

detail.what: How much rain falls in a place's wettest month, and how much that month varies from year to year, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: Checked against the largest one-day rainfall of each year at 248 weather stations (NOAA GHCN-Daily): rank agreement 0.69, with 0.70 in the United States and 0.42 in Europe.
detail.next: Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports.

coverage.hazard.saline_intrusion.label: Coastal elevation and IPCC sea-level rise

detail.what: How low and how close to the coast a place lies, raised by the sea-level rise the IPCC projects.
detail.why: Checked against the salinity measured in coastal groundwater at 3,400 monitoring points (Thorslund and van Vliet, 2020): rank agreement 0.10, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Real salinity depends on the rock, on pumping and on the nearest source of salt water, which elevation and distance to the coast do not capture.

detail.what: How much a place's rainfall changes under a climate scenario, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models. Drying and wetting both count.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year. Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How unevenly rain falls through the year, and how much it varies from year to year, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: It describes the climate rather than a damage, so testing it would prove nothing.
detail.next: Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How acidic the surface ocean is near a coastal or marine site, from the OceanSODA-ETHZ global record of ocean pH.
detail.why: It is already an observation, so there is nothing separate to test it against.
detail.next: For aquaculture, fisheries and other marine exposure only; it does not apply to inland sites or to buildings.

detail.what: Whether a site lies within reach of a mapped glacial lake, scaled by the lake's size, from a global inventory of 117,000 glacial lakes (GIGLak).
detail.why: Outbursts happen at the mapped lakes themselves, so a test of nearness against past outbursts would be circular. It is a reference layer, like volcano and earthquake zones.
detail.next: A nearness screen, not a model of where flood water flows: it includes places near a lake but not downstream of it.

detail.what: How prone the ground at a place is to landslides, from slope and geology, using NASA's global landslide susceptibility map (LHASA).
detail.why: Checked against 9,500 landslides in NASA's Global Landslide Catalog: hit rate 0.95, and places rated high or above see 11 times more landslides.
detail.next: NASA used the same catalogue to develop the map, so this repeats the map's published accuracy rather than a fresh test.

detail.what: How fast the ground is sinking, measured by satellite radar (Copernicus European Ground Motion Service, 2020–2024, 100 m), on a scale of 0 to 20 mm a year. Outside its coverage a published susceptibility class (Herrera, 2021) is shown as an indicator.
detail.why: The sinking rate fitted on 2020–2021 ranks the rate the same 200,000 places showed in 2022–2024 with rank agreement 0.85.
detail.next: Measured ground motion exists for Europe only. Elsewhere the susceptibility class stays an indicator (0.21 and 0.10 in tests) and never leads a headline. A test of measured motion, not of damage.

detail.what: How far the shoreline is projected to retreat at a place under each scenario and year (JRC, Vousdoukas et al., 2020).
detail.why: Checked against the shoreline change seen by satellite from 1984 to 2016 at 11,252 places on 67 coasts: the 2050 score ranks observed erosion at 0.36.
detail.next: The projection was built partly from the same shoreline trends, so this shows consistency rather than independent skill; it stays an indicator.

detail.what: How much soil water erosion moves off cropland each year, in tonnes per hectare, from the GloSEM global model (about 100 m).
detail.why: Checked against sediment measured in 204 European river catchments (0.09) and 670 reservoirs worldwide (0.08). Allowing for how much eroded soil reaches the outlet moves these only to 0.11 and 0.12, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: The model gives erosion at a point, while the measurements cover whole catchments.

detail.what: Whether land is degraded under the UN Sustainable Development Goal indicator 15.3.1 (land cover, productivity and soil carbon), read from the Trends.Earth map.
detail.why: Checked against an independent 30 m land-productivity map (Li et al., 2025) at 4,000 points around the Mediterranean: rank agreement −0.17, the wrong direction, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Tested on two Mediterranean areas only.

coverage.hazard.avalanche.label: Terrain slope and a snow-climate estimate

detail.what: Whether slopes at a place are steep enough for avalanches to start, weighted by an estimate of snow climate from elevation and latitude.
detail.why: Checked against 4,367 avalanche start zones recorded in the Swiss Alps (SLF, 1970/71 to 2023/24): hit rate 0.67, rank agreement 0.29. Within high alpine terrain, from 1,500 m, the hit rate is 0.52, no better than chance.
detail.next: It separates mountains from lowlands and nothing more. Tested in Switzerland only.

detail.what: Whether a place has both permafrost (Obu et al., 2019) and the gentle slopes on which frozen, waterlogged soil creeps downhill.
detail.why: No observed record of soil creep exists at scale to test it against yet.
detail.next: A susceptibility flag, not a model of movement. It applies only where there is permafrost.

detail.what: The shaking a place has felt from recorded earthquakes, estimated from their size and distance (USGS and EMSC catalogues, with the Bakun–Wentworth intensity relation).
detail.why: A consistency check only (rank agreement 0.81 near the source, hit rate 0.96): the score is built from the same catalogue it is checked against. An independent test is pending.
detail.next: Earthquakes do not respond to climate; the score is the same in every scenario.

detail.what: How exposed a place is to a volcano's near-vent hazards and ash fall, from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program catalogue: about 1,200 volcanoes and the size of their recorded eruptions.
detail.why: Eruptions are too rare for a test at the level of a single place, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Hazard zones are circles around the volcano, with no wind or terrain. Where the catalogue records no eruption size, a moderate one (VEI 3) is assumed. No euro figure is published for it.

detail.what: How far air pollution exceeds the World Health Organization's 2021 air-quality guideline levels.
detail.why: No observed outcome record to test it against has been set up yet.
detail.next: Its coverage is limited.

coverage.limitation.water_management.label: Irrigation does not explain yields better than rain

detail.what: Water stress is scored from rainfall-based drought and soil moisture, not from the reservoirs farmers irrigate from. We tested whether stored basin water explains an irrigated crop's yield better than rainfall does; it does not.

The platform supplies none.

The figures come from the same physical-risk engine the entity uses in its own workspace. An exposure's headline hazard is its highest score among the hazards whose scale measures intensity for its kind of asset; the day's live readings, susceptibility classes and variability percentiles do not count. An exposure counts as sensitive when its headline score is at or above the stated at-risk threshold: the entity's own threshold for its template, your threshold for the rebuilt figure and the peer benchmark.

Each filed cell's share of sensitive exposure is set against the spread of that share across the regions of the cell's country (the middle half, from the 25th to the 75th percentile), read from the platform's standing hazard scores at the same basis. It needs locations only.

The filed template is rebuilt from your own granular data, and each difference is split by cause: different exposure, coverage, basis, risk assessment, and rows on one side only. A marked cell is a question for the entity, not a finding.

platform.feed.climate_reanalysis.label: Copernicus ERA5 and ERA5-Land climate reanalysis

detail.what: Global climate reanalysis from Copernicus and ECMWF: temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, frost and wind.
detail.why: It scores heat, drought, frost, soil water and wind. Global baselines for temperature, precipitation, soil moisture and frost are in place, so scoring is worldwide.

platform.feed.flood.label: ERA5-Land runoff, a stand-in flood source

detail.what: Total runoff from Copernicus ERA5-Land, standing in for river discharge since the Copernicus river-discharge data was withdrawn from the Climate Data Store in 2025.
detail.why: It was the input of an earlier flood model. The published flood score now reads the JRC river-flood hazard maps, so a refresh of this source does not change a filing.

detail.what: Flood depth at about 90 m for the 1-in-10, 1-in-100 and 1-in-500-year river floods, with the permanent-water mask, from the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre.
detail.why: It drives the flood score. It covers river flooding only: surface-water, flash and groundwater flooding are not covered, and the maps carry no flood defences, so they show the hazard, not the risk left behind defences.

detail.what: Active fires detected by the VIIRS satellite instruments, from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System.
detail.why: Heat readings from Sentinel-3 (thermal-infrared brightness temperature) are connected through the Copernicus Data Space and start once access to it is set up. They are brightness temperature, not the corrected land-surface temperature product.

detail.what: Air quality, dust and fire emissions from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, read when needed and not stored.
detail.why: It informs the risk view. Pollution reporting is outside the scope of the climate and nature filings.

platform.feed.imagery.label: Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 imagery

detail.what: Satellite radar (Sentinel-1) and optical imagery (Sentinel-2) from the Copernicus programme.
detail.why: The Sentinel-1 flood reading, radar backscatter and its change over seven days, is built and starts once access credentials for the Copernicus Data Space are in place; until readings arrive it shows as not yet available. Sentinel-2 vegetation readings are not yet in production.

detail.what: Tracks and strengths of tropical cyclones worldwide, from NOAA's International Best Track Archive.
detail.why: It drives the cyclone score. Sea-state data from Copernicus Marine is not yet connected.

detail.what: Thirty years (1991 to 2020) of daily minimum and maximum temperature at 2 m, read for each location when needed, from NASA POWER.
detail.why: Cold wave: the 1-in-10 coldest night and the location's 99.6 % design temperature, from the daily minima. Rising heat: the number of days at or above 30 °C, from the daily maxima.

platform.feed.geophysical.label: USGS earthquakes and Smithsonian volcano records

detail.what: Earthquake scores from the global USGS catalogue of earthquakes of magnitude 5.0 and above, with the European seismic hazard model as a background layer; and eruption records for the volcanoes the volcanic score is tested on.
detail.why: Earthquakes and volcanoes are geophysical, not climate-related, so they are outside the scope of the climate and nature filings.

platform.feed.fire_climatology.label: Fire weather index and burned-area history

detail.what: Days of extreme fire danger from 2006 to 2020 from the Copernicus Fire Weather Index (ECMWF), combined with burned-area history from 2001 to 2019 from the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the European Space Agency.
detail.why: It is the wildfire climatology behind the wildfire score, rebuilt once a year.

platform.feed.volcanic_gvp.label: Smithsonian Volcanoes of the World catalogue

detail.what: About 1,200 volcanoes active in roughly the last 12,000 years and about 11,000 catalogued eruptions with their explosive size, from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program.
detail.why: It drives the volcanic screening score for any address. Volcanoes are geophysical, so they are outside the scope of the climate and nature filings.

detail.what: Projected change in temperature, precipitation and near-surface wind against 1995 to 2014, for each warming pathway and period, as the average of four climate models with their spread, on a 2° grid.
detail.why: It drives the warming, rainfall-change and wind-change scores and the future years of the flood, cyclone and wildfire scores.

detail.what: The observed 1-in-10-year extreme still-water level at the nearest tide gauge, from 1,864 gauges with ten or more years of records between 1979 and 2020.
detail.why: It sets how high the sea can reach at a coastal site; sea-level rise from the IPCC's sixth assessment is added for future years. A site with no gauge within 250 km is not scored.

platform.feed.elevation_dem.label: Copernicus elevation model and the coastline

detail.what: Elevation and slope at each site, read when needed from the Copernicus global elevation model, and the distance to the coastline (Natural Earth).
detail.why: It feeds coastal flooding and saltwater intrusion (elevation and distance to the coast), and avalanche and soil creep (slope).

detail.what: Landslide susceptibility classes at about 1 km, from slope, geology, roads, fault zones and forest loss (NASA).
detail.why: It shows how prone the ground is to landslides, not a forecast of a landslide after rain, and it does not change with the climate scenario.

detail.what: Vertical ground movement measured by satellite radar at 100 m and calibrated against satellite-positioning stations, 2020 to 2024.
detail.why: It drives the subsidence score across the European Economic Area; outside its coverage the global susceptibility map is used.

detail.what: Subsidence susceptibility classes at about 1 km, from aquifer compaction, rock and soil type, groundwater depletion and urban load (Herrera-García and others, 2021).
detail.why: It is the subsidence score outside the coverage of the European Ground Motion Service.

detail.what: The probability of permafrost at about 1 km across the Northern Hemisphere north of 25°N (Obu and others, 2019, European Space Agency).
detail.why: It drives the permafrost thaw score and, with slope, the soil-creep score.

detail.what: Soil lost to water erosion, in tonnes per hectare a year at about 100 m (European Soil Data Centre; Borrelli and Panagos).
detail.why: It drives the soil erosion score.

detail.what: Whether land is degraded, stable or improving, from the global map behind the United Nations land-degradation indicator (Trends.Earth, Conservation International), read for each location when needed and not stored.
detail.why: It drives the soil degradation score.

platform.feed.coastal_erosion_liscoast.label: JRC shoreline-change projections for sandy coasts

detail.what: Projected long-term retreat of sandy coastlines under the RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 emission pathways in 2050 and 2100 (European Commission's Joint Research Centre; Vousdoukas and others, 2020).
detail.why: It drives the coastal erosion score for future years only: it has no value for today.

detail.what: The recent mean pH of the surface ocean on a global grid (OceanSODA-ETHZ, NOAA).
detail.why: It drives the ocean acidification score and applies only to coastal and marine assets.

detail.what: About 117,000 mapped glacial lakes with their area.
detail.why: It screens how close a site is to a glacial lake; it does not model the path an outburst flood would take.

detail.what: Annual forest loss worldwide (University of Maryland), read when a deforestation check runs and not stored.
detail.why: Deforestation checks are run again on each new release.

detail.what: The boundaries of the EU's Natura 2000 protected areas, from one annual release of the European Environment Agency; EU coverage.
detail.why: It flags your sites and sourcing plots in or near a Natura 2000 area, for biodiversity reporting. The data may be reused, including commercially, with acknowledgement, which is shown.

detail.what: Protected areas outside the EU from OpenStreetMap, used where the World Database on Protected Areas needs a licence.
detail.why: It is community-sourced with uneven coverage: a screening layer, not an agency source, and labelled as such.

detail.what: Protected areas worldwide, the counterpart to Natura 2000 outside the EU (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN, Protected Planet).
detail.why: It is available under a licence through IBAT; connecting it is pending.

detail.what: Areas conserved by means other than protection, the companion to the World Database on Protected Areas (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN).
detail.why: It widens the coverage of biodiversity reporting. Like the World Database on Protected Areas it is licensed through IBAT; connecting it is pending.

detail.what: Sites of significance for global biodiversity (KBA Partnership).
detail.why: It is licensed commercially through IBAT together with the World Database on Protected Areas; once the licence is in place it is loaded from the licensed file with the other protected areas.

detail.what: Legal entity identifiers (LEI) from the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation.
detail.why: A change renames an entity; it does not change a risk score.
